questions.prompt: A leader in term 6 sees that an entry from term 4 is now stored on a majority. No entries from term 6 exist yet. What does it do?
options: Marks the term 4 entry committed, since it is on a majority
Rewrites the entry with term 6 and then commits it
Waits, and commits it only once an entry from term 6 after it is on a majority
Asks the term 4 leader to confirm the commit
questions.explanation: Figure 8 shows an old-term entry on a majority can still be overwritten by a server with a newer last term. Only current-term entries are committed by counting; earlier ones are committed indirectly beneath them. Rewriting an entry's term is never allowed: entries keep the term they were created in.

questions.prompt: In Figure 8 (d), why can S5 win the election even though S1, S2 and S3 hold the term 2 entry at index 2?
options: Because S5's last entry has term 3, which is more up-to-date than the term 2 entries on its voters
Because S5 has the highest server ID
questions.explanation: The up-to-date check compares last terms first. S2, S3 and S4 have last terms 2, 2 and 1, all below 3, so they vote for S5. S5's log is not longer: S2 and S3 have the same length.

questions.prompt: Why does a newly elected leader append a no-op entry at the start of its term?
options: To reset every follower's election timer
To overwrite any uncommitted entries on followers
Because AppendEntries cannot be sent with an empty Entries slice
So it can commit an entry from its own term promptly, which also commits all inherited entries and tells it the true commitIndex
questions.explanation: Under the current-term rule, inherited entries cannot commit until a current-term entry does. A no-op makes that happen without waiting for a client. Heartbeats already reset timers and can be empty, so those options are tempting but not the reason.
